title: Imperatives with pronouns, both aspects
goal: Give commands with object pronouns in the right order and aspect.

blocks.text: At B1 the imperative is mostly about combinations: verb + one or two weak pronouns, the second accent, the elided vowel, and choosing aspect. **Πες μου**, **δώσ' το μου**, **φέρ' τα**, **πάρε με τηλέφωνο**, **κοίταξέ το**. With two pronouns after an imperative, the usual order is accusative then genitive (δώσ' το μου), though genitive first also occurs (δώσε μου το).

blocks.title: Έλα, άντε, άσ' το: commands in everyday talk
blocks.text: Some imperatives have become all-purpose words. **Έλα** 'come' is how many Greeks answer the phone when they know who is calling, and it also means 'come on!' or 'no way!' depending on the tone. **Άντε** 'go on, hurry up' urges someone along (**άντε, θα αργήσουμε**). **Άσ' το** (from αφήνω) is 'forget it, leave it'. **Για πες** 'go on, tell me' invites a story, and **Κάτσε** (from κάθομαι) is 'sit down' or 'hang on'. In the kitchen, recipes and grandmothers speak almost entirely in perfective imperatives: **ρίξε** 'throw in', **ανακάτεψε** 'stir', **άφησέ το να βράσει** 'let it boil'.

blocks.title: Aspect in commands
items: Perfective for a single, specific instruction: Κλείσε την πόρτα.
Imperfective for a general rule, a habit, or 'go on, keep doing': Τρώγε λιγότερο. Γράφε μου! Έλα, προχώρα!
Prohibition: μην + perfective for a specific act (Μην το πεις), μην + imperfective to stop an action in progress or for a general rule (Μην τρέχεις, Μην καπνίζεις).

blocks.title: Κεφτέδες με τη γιαγιά
blocks.en:
— Niko, come into the kitchen! Today you'll learn to make meatballs.
— OK, Grandma. What should I do?
— First wash your hands. Then take the mince out of the fridge and put it in a big bowl.
— I've put it in. Now?

— Chop the onion very finely. Not like that, watch me! Hold the knife the way I do. Well done. Now throw it into the mince.
— Shall I put the bread in too?
— Yes, but first wet it a little and squeeze it out well. And give me the mint, so I can show you how much we put in. Bring it here... That's enough.

— And salt?
— Put in a teaspoon. Now mix it all together with your hands. Don't rush! Knead, keep kneading, until it becomes a nice mixture.
— Grandma, I'm tired!
— Don't moan at me! Keep going a little more. Now make little balls and roll them in the flour.

— And then we fry them?
— Yes. But watch out for the oil, it's hot. Leave this part to me. You set the table and call Grandpa.
— OK, Grandma. Shall I put out glasses too?
— Yes, and bring the salad from the fridge as well. Don't forget it! And tell Grandpa to switch off the TV. Tell him we're eating in ten minutes!

gloss.ρίξ: ρίχνω — throw in! (ρίξε, elided before το)
gloss.στύψ: στύβω — squeeze out! (στύψε, elided before το)
gloss.Άσ: αφήνω — leave it! (άσε, elided before το)

items.why: Second accent when the stress would fall more than three syllables from the end.
An ongoing request: imperfective.
A specific act: μην + perfective.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Give it (n.) to me!*
items.why: Pronouns follow the imperative, usually accusative then genitive; δώσε elides to δώσ' before το.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Tell me!* (to a friend)
items.why: πες is the perfective imperative of λέω; the genitive pronoun follows.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Tell us!* (polite or plural)
items.why: Plural imperative of λέω: πείτε (colloquial πέστε).

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Wait for me!* (to a friend)
items.why: Adding με would put the stress four syllables from the end, so a second accent goes on the last syllable of the verb.
φέρε + τους (masc. acc. pl.); the final -ε is often elided.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Don't tell him (it)!* (this one time)
items.why: After μην the pronouns move in front of the verb, genitive before accusative; a specific act takes the perfective.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Don't shout!* (stop it, to a friend)
items.why: Stopping an action in progress: μην + imperfective.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Open the window, please.* (polite)
items.why: Polite plural perfective imperative: ανοίξτε.
Colloquial imperative of αφήνω is άσε (formal άφησε); before το it elides to άσ' το.

items.prompt: Say in Greek, one word: *Keep reading!* (go on, to a friend)
items.why: 'Keep doing' is the imperfective imperative.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Show it (f.) to me!*
items.why: δείξε + τη (fem. acc.) + μου; accusative first is the usual order.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *Sit down!* (to a friend)
items.why: κάθομαι has active-looking imperatives: κάθισε, colloquial κάτσε; polite καθίστε.

items.prompt: General advice to a child: ___ στον δρόμο!
items.why: A general, ongoing instruction takes the imperfective; πρόσεξε warns about one specific danger.
With a positive imperative the weak pronoun always follows the verb.
μην + subjunctive, and the pronoun goes before the verb as with any subjunctive.
Polite plural perfective imperative of περνάω.
Accusative then genitive, both after the verb.
Plural addressee, one specific act: perfective plural κλείστε.
A standing rule: μην + imperfective; δεν never negates commands.
One call: perfective imperative, pronoun after it.
